newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU raids Opel, Mercedes in car pricing probe.
newsitem.headline: EU raids Opel, Mercedes in car pricing probe.

text.p: The European Commission has raided some offices of German carmaker Mercedes Benz AG and the Adam Opel subsidiary of General Motors Corp. as part of a probe into pricing irregularities, an EU source said Friday.
Both carmakers acknowledged that their offices had been visited but said the probe was very limited.
Mercedes-Benz confirmed that the European Commission searched some of its dealers' offices but said its headquarters in Stuttgart was not visited.
Opel said the European Commission had searched two of its offices in the Netherlands late last year but it, too, said its headquarters had not been searched.

"There have been no searches and there are no searches being conducted at Adam Opel AG," Opel said in answer to a query. "The European Commission, however, searched through offices at one Dutch Opel dealer and at Opel Niederlande late last year."

News of the raids emerged Friday as the commission, the European Union's executive body, released details of car price differentials across 12 of the EU's 15 member countries, excluding Greece, Finland and Denmark.
Commission data up until Nov. 1, 1996, showed that 23 of the EU's 75 best-selling models were cheapest in the Netherlands while 21 were cheapest in Portugal.

The Commission said parallel trade in cars -- when customers try to buy vehicles elswehere in the EU when price differences make it attractive to do so -- was being blocked in Germany, Belgium, Spain and the Netherlands.

The raids, in connection with alleged irregularities in vehicle pricing and distribution arrangements by the two car manufacturers, were on similar grounds to current commission investigations into Volkswagen and its Audi subsidiary, the source said.
"It was found that final customers still encounter obstacles in certain member states," the commission said in a statement.
The raids on Mercedes related to sales in all four named countries while those at Opel related only to Dutch sales, the source said.

If the commission were to find the companies guilty of malpractice, it could strip them of anti-trust exemptions related to their distribution agreements, a move which would open tightly restricted vehicle distribution arrangements to greater competition, the source said.
